newsitem.title: USA: Mrs. Clinton honors working mothers at White House.
newsitem.headline: Mrs. Clinton honors working mothers at White House.

text.p: Hillary Rodham Clinton paid tribute to working mothers on Monday, and unwitttingly illustrated the problems they face when one of the honourees had to leave a White House luncheon early to attend her daughter's dance recital.
Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick slipped out of the luncheon in East Room before the first lady finished her remarks about challenges for women who work both in the home and outside of it.
"She (Gorelick) had to go to her daughter's ballet recital," explained Judsen Culbreth, editor-in-chief of Working Mother Magazine, prompting a ripple of appreciative laughter from the guests.

Gorelick, 46, was one of 25 women named by Working Mother magazine this month as "The 25 Most Influential Working Mothers" in America. However, Gorelick announced recently that she will be leaving her administration job, and department officials said she wanted to spend more time with her 8-year-old son and 3-year-old daughter.

Clinton, the mother of 16-year-old daughter Chelsea, was also one of the magazine's honourees and hosted the White House lunch on Monday for them and about 150 other working mothers from a cross-section of American life.
Many were high-powered Washingtonians, including Gorelick, Environmental Protection Agency administrator Carol Browner, and Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky.

Others were people Clinton had met in her travels as first lady, including Lisa Thomas, a single mother of four who makes $6 an hour and drove about 200 miles to Washington from Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to attend the luncheon.

In praising the women, Clinton said, "behind every smiling face you will see you can imagine there have been a lot of sleepless nights, a lot of juggling, a lot of challenges that have been balanced as best as anyone could."

The first lady, author of a book about family issues, said the problems working mothers faced needed to become part of the political debate. Many American women work out of economic necessity and 75 percent of them earn less than $25,000 a year, making it difficult to afford good child care, she said.

"We need to start thinking about how to create a balance in our lives, and in our society, that will enable working mothers -- those we honour today and millions who will never be honoured -- to feel that they can succeed both at home and or work," Clinton said.
